t.5.65.1: Thus addressed by the great-souled Rāghava, Hanumān reported to Rāghava everything that Sītā had said.
t.5.65.3: Jānakī, who had been sleeping peacefully with you, awoke first; then a crow, suddenly flying up, tore at her between the breasts.
t.5.65.2: O bull among men, the divine Jānakī told me this token of recognition, an event that took place long ago at Citrakūṭa, exactly as it happened.
t.5.65.4: And in turn, O elder brother of Bharata, you fell asleep in the lap of the queen; and then, it is said, that bird again caused distress to the queen.
t.5.65.5: Then, coming back once more, it tore at her fiercely, it is said; and then you were awakened, drenched with her blood.
t.5.65.6: And you, O scorcher of foes, sleeping happily beside the queen, were awakened, it is said, by her as she was being constantly harassed by that very crow.
t.5.65.8: O timid one, by whom was the space between your breasts torn with the tips of his claws? Who is it that plays with an enraged five-headed serpent?
t.5.65.7: Seeing her wounded between the breasts, O mighty-armed one, you, enraged like a venomous serpent and hissing with breath, spoke to her.
t.5.65.9: Looking about, you suddenly saw the crow, standing facing me alone, its sharp claws stained with blood.
t.5.65.10: That crow, the best of birds, was, it is said, the son of Śakra; roaming swiftly over the earth, he was equal to the wind in speed.
t.5.65.11: Then, O mighty-armed one, with your eyes rolling in anger, you set your mind on cruel intent toward that crow, O best of the wise.
t.5.65.12: Taking a blade of darbha grass from the mat, you charged it with the brahmāstra; and it blazed up like the flaming fire at the end of time, turned toward the bird.
t.5.65.13: You then hurled that blazing blade of darbha grass at the crow, and the blazing darbha went in pursuit of the crow.
t.5.65.14: Abandoned by his father and by all the gods and great seers, he wandered through the three worlds but found no protector.
t.5.65.15: O Kākutstha, you, the giver of refuge, protected him out of compassion as he lay fallen on the ground, having come to you for refuge, though he deserved death.
t.5.65.16: "A missile cannot be rendered fruitless," thinking thus, O Rāghava, he then destroyed the right eye of that crow.
t.5.65.17: O Rāma, having paid homage to you and to King Daśaratha, the crow, released then, went back to the sky, his dwelling place.
t.5.65.18: Thus, though you are the foremost of those versed in weapons, mighty and of noble character as well, why, O Rāghava, do you not loose your weapon against the rākṣasas?
t.5.65.19: Neither the Nāgas nor the Gandharvas, neither the Asuras nor the hosts of the Maruts, O Rāma, are able to stand before you or to resist you.
t.5.65.21: Or Lakṣmaṇa, scorcher of foes, taking up his brother's command, why does he not protect me? Why does Rāghava, best of men, not protect me?
t.5.65.20: If you, so full of valour, have any concern for me, let Rāvaṇa be swiftly slain in battle with well-sharpened arrows.
t.5.65.22: Those two tigers among men are capable, equal in splendour to Vāyu and Agni, unassailable even by the gods; for what reason do they neglect me?
t.5.65.23: Without doubt, some great misdeed of mine alone must exist, since those two scorchers of foes, capable and united as they are, pay no heed to me.
t.5.65.24: Having heard the piteous words of Vaidehī, spoken with tears, I once again spoke these words to that noble lady.
t.5.65.25: O queen, I swear to you by the truth: Rāma has turned away from all else in his grief for you, and with Rāma overwhelmed by sorrow, Lakṣmaṇa too is tormented.
t.5.65.26: Somehow you have been found, my lady; this is no time for grieving. This very moment, O beautiful one, you shall see the end of your sorrows.
t.5.65.27: Those two princes, tigers among men and subduers of their foes, their zeal kindled by the sight of you, will reduce Laṅkā to ashes.
t.5.65.28: And having slain in battle the fierce Rāvaṇa together with his kinsmen, the mighty-armed Rāghava will surely lead you to his own city.
t.5.65.29: O faultless lady, you should give me that token of recognition which Rāma would know, one that will awaken his joy.
t.5.65.30: Having looked around in all directions, she untied from her garment this jewel, the excellent ornament that fastened her braid, and gave it to me, O mighty one.
t.5.65.31: Having received the divine jewel for your sake, O best of the Raghus, and having bowed to her with my head, I hastened on my return.
t.5.65.32: Seeing me resolved upon departing and growing in size, the fair-complexioned daughter of Janaka, wretched, her face full of tears, spoke to me in a voice choked with weeping.
t.5.65.33: O Hanumān, convey my wishes for their well-being to both Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, who resemble lions, and to Sugrīva together with his ministers, to all of them.
t.5.65.34: You should bring it about that the mighty-armed Rāghava rescues me from this confinement in a flood of sorrow.
t.5.65.35: Having gone into Rāma's presence, you should tell him of this fierce surge of my grief and of the threats made against me by these Rākṣasas. And may your path be auspicious, O foremost hero among the monkeys.
t.5.65.36: O lion among kings, these are the words that your noble Sītā spoke to you in sorrow. Understanding what I have told you, trust that Sītā is well and wholly safe.
